To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we present a distributed algorithm for multi robot connectivity in unknown environments, where robots share local connectivity information without merging their maps, and use their own navigation and exploration to acquire information about the environment, and heuristics to plan their exploration to achieve connectivity among a set of sparsely positioned towers.

(1) we present a distributed connectivity algorithm that does not require map merging, (2) we introduce a tethering algorithm that solves the problem of tethering a single agent to a team of robots, (3) we demonstrate our algorithms in simulation and with physical robots, (4) we show that our tethering algorithm is robust to errors in the distance model, and (5) we demonstrate that our connectivity algorithm is scalable to large numbers of robots.

we propose a distributed algorithm that allows mobile robots to achieve connectivity in an unknown environment and use this team to locate and tether an agent without the need to communicate with it, using only RSSI measurements.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the problem of deploying a team of mobile robots to establish connectivity among static towers in an unknown environment, and then to locate an autonomous agent using only RSSI measurements.
the deployment of a team of mobile robots to connect a group of static towers in an unknown environment, and the subsequent tethering of an autonomous agent to the robots.
multi robot coordination in unknown environments.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
we have successfully demonstrated a distributed algorithm for multi robot connectivity and tethering in a realistic environment.
our work provides an effective solution for the problem of multi robot map merging in unknown environments.
our algorithm is able to achieve the connectivity goal in a variety of environments, and is able to successfully tether an agent to the robots in the same environments.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we contribute a multi robot algorithm to achieve connectivity among static towers, using a tethering algorithm that does not require any communication from the tethered agent, nor the need to know the agent's position in global coordinates.

we have developed a novel distributed algorithm that enables a team of mobile robots to connect to a set of static communication towers in an unknown environment without the need for global localization, and then use this team to locate and tether an autonomous agent, without the need to communicate with the agent.
we present a novel algorithm for solving the problem of positioning robots in unknown environments, and then tethering an agent to the robot network using only RSSI measurements.
The main takeaway from our work is that

a team of robots, initially not knowing their own or their teammates’ position, can be deployed in unknown environments and achieve connectivity among static towers and tether to an agent without the agent communicating with the robot team.

we have developed a distributed algorithm for a team of mobile robots to connect to a set of static communication towers, without knowing the environment, tower locations or initial positions of the robots, and without the agent communicating to the robots.

a team of robots can achieve connectivity among static towers, and use this connectivity to position and tether to an agent in an unknown environment, without requiring the agent to be able to communicate with the robots.
